en: The Chapter on Similes, Part One: The Lion Section.
4. The Question of the House-Pigeon “Venerable Nāgasena, when you say that ‘one quality of a house-pigeon should be adopted,’ which is that one quality that should be adopted?

“Just as, great king, a house-pigeon dwelling in another’s home does not take note of any of their belongings, but dwells with equanimity and much mindfulness; even so, great king, a monk who has gone forth into homelessness should dwell with equanimity toward all the requisites of a monk—whether robes, alms-food, lodging, or medicinal requisites for the sick—and he should dwell with much mindfulness.”
In the same way, great king, when a practitioner, a follower of yoga, has entered another’s family, he should not seize upon the sign of the women or men there—
whether in their beds, seats, clothing, ornaments, enjoyments, possessions, or varieties of food;
he should remain equanimous and maintain the perception of himself as a renunciant.
“Great King, this is one quality that should be adopted from the house-pigeon.
This was said, Great King, by the Blessed One, the God above Gods, in the Cūḷanāradajāta:
For the sake of nourishment or for food,
one should eat and consume in moderation,
and not set one’s mind on physical beauty.”
The fourth question: On the House-Pigeon.
